podcast.title: Managed by Bill Drummond
podcast.body: Brilliant was a band whose guitarist was Jimmy Cauty, and they were managed by Bill Drummond, who would later form The KLF with Cauty. "Coddy was the guitarist and a band called Brilliant, who was also managed by Drummond."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Glam Rock Catalyst (1971)
xref.body: In March 1971, T-Rex appeared on the hugely important British TV show "Top of the Pops." During this performance, Marc Bolan, the band's frontman, wore satin clothes and was covered with glitter dust, an event that David Bowie watched at home and found "brilliant," marking it as "the beginning of glam rock" and inspiring Bowie to pursue a similar direction. "In March 1971, T-Rex appeared on top of the pops, the hugely important British TV show."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Live Radio Improv (1987)
xref.body: In 1987, during an interview on live radio, Mojo Nixon improvised a song on the spot when asked why people should see him in a club instead of David Bowie in a stadium. "He picked up his guitar and improvised a song on the spot on live radio. And it was brilliant."

xref.title: BBC Documentary and Book About Her Death
xref.body: The details behind Kirsty MacColl's death are explored in a BBC documentary titled "Who Killed Kristi McCall" and a book by her sister, Jean, called "Sun on the Water, the brilliant life and tragic death of Kristi McCall." "If you're interested in the details behind Kristi's death, there's a BBC documentary called Who Killed Kristi McCall. And there's a book called Sun on the Water, the brilliant life and tragic death of Kristi McCall by her sister, Jean."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Brilliant Beginning, Debacle End
xref.body: Velvet Revolver's story was characterized by a brilliant start but ended in a "debacle," which was attributed almost entirely to Scott Weiland's issues. "The whole Velvet Revolver story, which began so brilliantly and ended in such a debacle, thanks almost entirely to Scott."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Commercialization of the Fuzz Pedal
xref.body: After hearing the distinctive fuzzy guitar sound on Marty Robbins' "Don't Worry," Gibson Guitars approached Grady Martin to develop a commercial product. Martin, along with Glenn Snottie and Revis Hobbs, designed the circuit, and Gibson manufactured the first-ever fuzz pedal, the Maestro FZ1 Fuzz tone. This product made distortion widely available to guitarists. "When the prototype was ready, Grady and Glenn Snottie took the contraption, which had taken on the form of a foot pedal, to Gibson's offices in Chicago. They took one listen and said, this is brilliant. We'll take it."

xref.title: David Bowie's Endorsement
xref.body: Despite their struggle for commercial success across four albums before disbanding in 1975, Fanny garnered high praise from David Bowie, who considered them "brilliant." "Like I said, Bowie thought they were brilliant."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

xref.title: Don Letts' Theory Connection
xref.body: Don Letts, a British DJ and filmmaker close to The Clash during the original punk scene, developed a theory that the optimal lifespan for most bands is seven to nine years. He suggests that this period allows for birth, rise, peak, and then explosion due to internal pressures like creative differences. The Clash are cited as an example of a brilliant band for their time that, despite multi-million dollar offers, never reunited to record new material. "He was especially close with the clash. And he has a theory. He believes the average and proper lifespan of most bands is seven years, nine at the outside."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Life and Artistic Path
xref.body: Richard Hell, born Richard Myers in Kentucky, initially moved to New York with the ambition of becoming a poet before becoming captivated by the burgeoning punk scene at CBGB. "Richard, his real name was Richard Myers, was a member of several New York punk bands who hung out at CBGB, the brilliant television and the heartbreakers featuring the doomed Johnny Thunders, ex of the New York dolls. Richard was born in Kentucky but moved to New York with plans of being a poet."

xref.title: Enduring Quality of Music
xref.body: Much of The Beatles' music remains brilliant, even though most of it is more than 50 years old. "I mean, most of the Beatles music is still brilliant, even though much of it is more than 50 years old."

srcs.episode: Trying to be a Superstar in the 21st Century

xref.title: Glam Rock Genesis
xref.body: David Bowie was significantly inspired by Mark Bolan, a former folk musician who formed the psych band T-Rex. Bolan's appearance on "Top of the Pops" in March 1971, wearing satin clothes covered with glitter dust, struck Bowie as brilliant and marked the beginning of Glam Rock. "This was the beginning of Glam Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Guitar Virtuosity and Frank Zappa's Praise (Unspecified Year)
xref.body: Warren Cuccurullo was a member of Frank Zappa's band, and Zappa himself considered him "brilliant" for his ability to play even the most difficult arrangements perfectly. This skill was particularly impressive given the complexity of Zappa's music. He was named-checked four times on Zappa's "Joe's Garage" album, including in the songs "Catholic Girls" and "Cruisin' for Burgers." "Zappa thought he was brilliant because no matter how difficult an arrangement was, Warren could play it perfectly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Punk Fashion
xref.body: Richard Hell's distinctive safety-pin-adorned clothing caught the attention of UK band manager Malcolm McLaren in New York. McLaren subsequently brought this "safety pin look" to Britain, incorporating it into his clothing shop "Sex," which became a popular spot for disaffected youth. "So Richard wore his clothes until they fell apart. In fact, he wore them even after they fell apart, holding things together with safety pins. This went a wannabe band manager from the UK named Malcolm McLaren, saw Richard in New York and thought he had brilliant fashion sense."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influential Songwriter and Versatility
xref.body: As a singer-songwriter, PJ Harvey was among the most influential of the 90s alt-rock women, known for her honest, often dark, theatrical, and sometimes punk-like material. Her brilliant versatility allows her to fearlessly explore diverse musical forms. "She is brilliantly versatile."

xref.title: LA-Based Band
xref.body: Fever 333 is identified as a band originating from Los Angeles, featuring vocalist Jason Aalon Butler. "There's LA's Fever 333 featuring vocalist Jason O'on Butler, militia Fox, brilliant."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mansinth – Marilyn Manson's Absinthe Brand
xref.body: Marilyn Manson launched his own brand of absinthe called Mansinth, which is produced in Germany. Absinthe, historically known for its psychoactive reputation and associated with figures like Oscar Wilde and Vincent Van Gogh, experienced a revival in the 1990s. Mansinth garnered significant acclaim, winning a gold medal at the San Francisco World's Spirits Competition in March 2008. The product is described as expensive and was not available in Canada at the time of the discussion. "Mansinth is Marilyn Manson's brand, which is made in Germany and it is absolutely brilliant."

xref.title: Pioneering Safety Pin Fashion
xref.body: Richard Hell was so poor that his clothes were literally falling apart, and he held them together with safety pins. Malcolm McLaren was "particularly taken" with this look, considering it a "brilliant fashion statement" which he then brought back to England to sell at his store. "This guy was so poor that his clothes were literally falling apart and the only way he could wear anything was to hold his clothes together with safety pins."

xref.title: Singing Career Beginnings
xref.body: Florence Foster Jenkins began her singing career with recitals in 1912, utilizing funds from an inheritance to support her artistic endeavors. She believed herself to be a brilliant opera singer, despite lacking a sense of rhythm, pitch, tone, or pacing, or any discernible musical talent. "She persisted using the funds from an inheritance to further her singing career, beginning with some recitals in 1912."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Teenage Diagnoses and Ban from Colorado
xref.body: Diagnosed with schizophrenia at age fifteen, Nancy was also brilliant and enrolled in university in Colorado at sixteen. However, she was thrown out due to "bad and weird behavior," including an arrest for trying to buy pot and accusations of theft. As a result of her issues, she was banished from the state to avoid legal consequences. "Nancy was diagnosed with schizophrenia when she was 15."
